parts.text:
I'm deciding whether to compute these growth statistics by hand or write a quick script, and lean toward doing it manually since it's feasible with careful arithmetic. I'm now going through the control group plant measurements across the five time points to set up the calculation.

Noting that one control value (119.5 for P04 at day 6) looks like an outlier that I'll need to account for, then recording the drought group's measurements the same way. I compute day-12 means for both groups (~17.62 cm control vs ~12.54 cm drought), then calculate total growth from day 0 to day 12 for each plant, finding control plants gained about 12.82 cm on average while drought plants gained about 7.55 cm, meaning drought growth is roughly 59% of control growth.

I flag that P04's day-6 value (119.5 cm) is clearly a data error given it's surrounded by 8.2 and 15.32, so I estimate a plausible corrected value around 11.95 cm without letting it affect the day-12 endpoint comparison. I also check baseline day-0 heights across groups (control ~4.80 cm, drought ~4.99 cm) to confirm starting conditions were roughly similar, and note the small sample size (n=4 per group) means any statistical test like a t-test would have limited power.

Running a Welch's t-test on day-12 height data, I get means of 17.6175 (control) vs 12.535 (drought), with standard deviations of about 0.618 and 0.193 respectively. The resulting t-statistic comes out around 15.7 with roughly 3.6 degrees of freedom, which corresponds to a very small p-value, likely under 0.001 — I should present this as approximate given the tiny sample size, while also flagging that the day-6 outlier shouldn't be folded into any trajectory-based growth analysis without correction.

I should also note that these calculations were done by hand rather than via script, offer to verify with code if needed, and highlight study limitations like the small n=4 per group, lack of randomization/blocking information, and repeated-measures design. I'll also mention the day-12 leaf counts (control mean 7.25 vs drought mean 6) and plan to structure the final answer with headings, a summary table, and a link to the data file.

**Yes, the drought plants grew more slowly.** The difference is large and consistent across all four drought plants, but the sample is small (4 plants per group), so treat the size of the effect as approximate.

The numbers below are my hand calculations from the file at [greenhouse_trial.csv](workspace-file:/home/user/clio-cloudlive-ws/greenhouse_trial.csv). I have not run them through a script.

| Measure | Control (n=4) | Drought (n=4) |
|---|---|---|
| Height, day 0 (mean, cm) | 4.80 | 4.99 |
| Height, day 12 (mean, cm) | 17.62 | 12.54 |
| Growth, day 0 to 12 (mean, cm) | 12.82 | 7.55 |
| Leaf count, day 12 (mean) | 7.25 | 6.00 |

- Drought plants gained about 41% less height over the 12 days (about 5.3 cm less on average).
- At day 12, control plants averaged about 5.1 cm taller.
- Every drought plant ended shorter than every control plant on day 12. The control range is 17.14–18.52 cm and the drought range is 12.35–12.79 cm.
- A Welch t-test on day-12 height gives t ≈ 15.7 with about 3.6 degrees of freedom. That is a very strong separation, but with four plants per group the estimate is still rough.

The drought plants also started slightly taller on day 0 (4.99 vs 4.80 cm), so the gap is not caused by a head start.

**Problems in the data:**

1. **Impossible value for P04 on day 6.** The control plant P04 reads 119.5 cm. Its neighbours are 8.2 cm on day 3 and 15.32 cm on day 9, so this looks like a data-entry error, possibly 11.95 or a similar value. It does not affect the day-12 comparison, but it would distort any analysis that uses the whole growth curve, such as area under the curve or a mean across days. I have not changed it. It should be checked against the original notes.
2. **Missing context.** The file has no units metadata, no description of how plants were assigned to treatments, no pot or bench position, and no info on how watering was controlled. Without these I can't tell whether the four plants per group are independent or share a tray.
3. **Small n.** Four plants per group is enough to see a clear effect here, but not enough to estimate its size precisely or to check the assumptions of a t-test.

If you can tell me how the plants were assigned and whether the day-6 value can be checked, I can rerun the comparison with the corrected value and a model that accounts for repeated measures on each plant.
